Messages.Author: BobbyDoc
Messages.Body:
Hi,

In a V:EKN constructed deck tournament, each Methuselah's library deck
must have between sixty and ninety cards.

Maybe little stupid question, but why 60-90 ?

What was the reasons for choosing these boundaries?
Was 50 to few? 100 to many?

My guess is that these boundaries was arbitrary chosen, but I could be
wrong.

Long discussions and tests may have come to these values. If so I'm
very interested (yes, I like statistical tests) in those.

Of course I'm also interested in the lower boundary of the crypt. Was
that boundary chosen in the same matter as the deck limit?

I notice there is no upper limit for the crypt. Do this mean I can
come to a tournament with a crypt of 50000 vamps and a deck full of
Recruitment's? Or do that fall under unsportsmanlike behaviour?

Regards
Robert

On 26 jun, 10:11, BobbyDoc <robert_dokto...@hotmail.com> wrote:

> In a V:EKN constructed deck tournament, each Methuselah's library deck
> must have between sixty and ninety cards.
>

In a normal game libraries are 40 to 40+ (10*number of players), since
you only play 4 or 5 player games in tournements, library max should
be 80 (4 players) or 90 (5 players.) Since you can't change your deck,
they opted for the 90 card maximum. Where the 60 minimum comes from I
don't really know.

>
<snip>

> I notice there is no upper limit for the crypt. Do this mean I can
> come to a tournament with a crypt of 50000 vamps and a deck full of
> Recruitment's? Or do that fall under unsportsmanlike behaviour?

IIRC, LSJ has said that you have to be able to randomise you crypt in
a way that's fast enough to do in in max. a couple of minutes.

Messages.Author: Slytherin
Messages.Body:
IANLSJ, but I was under the impression that 60-90 was chosen, as for
ordinary play, the minimum decksize is 40, and maximum is 40 + (10 *
number of players).

As a tournament table should ideally be 4 or 5 players 40 + (10 * 4) =
80, 40 +(10 * 5) = 90.

60 minimum allows for a sufficient randomisation factor for the cards
(even the twister strategy to get the effective deck down to 40 again
can struggle, and can certainly jam for a turn or two).

In the case of vampires, again it is the assumption that 12 allows for
randomisation factor of selected minions, but having no upper limit on
crypt size allows you to play a large number of minions strategy.

You could come to a tournament with 50000 vamps and 90 recruitments,
but I think you'd struggle, and therefore it wouldn't be
unsportsmanlike.

I think you'd need to speak with Richard Garfield about why minimums
where chosen, and why they where set as they were. MTG and VTES both
started with a minimum of 40. In MTG this only remains for limited
play, in VTES it remains for casual and limited. However, in MTG they
also have card limits, and 60 is effectively also the maximum deck
size (also there is no maximum). In VTES, having a maximum forces card
choice and puts another limit on resources (which I believe the game
to be about).

Andy
VEKN Setite Ruler of Cambridge

Messages.Author: Bram Vink
Messages.Body:


I would assume that in the testing phase of the game, there was a
conscious choice to make running out of cards a viable risk (hence the
decksize being dependent on how many players there were) I think it's
fair to assume that the amount of cards has been the result of
playing, and seeing how many cards were played, then a simplification
of that.
So the original rules stated: 40+10/player is the maximum size.

However, since in a tournament it isnt a good idea to have people
alter their decks between rounds based on how many players they have
to play against, a basic standard had to be set, in accordance to the
rules above, taking into account the tournament maximum of players/
table is 5, the upper limit was set at 90.
Since the minimum amount of players to play the game is 2, the lower
limit is 60.

That's how I'd assume things went,
Cheers,
B

Messages.Author: witness1
Messages.Body:
On Jun 26, 8:02 am, Bram Vink <jja.v...@hccnet.nl> wrote:
> On Jun 26, 10:11 am, BobbyDoc <robert_dokto...@hotmail.com> wrote:
> I would assume that in the testing phase of the game, there was a
> conscious choice to make running out of cards a viable risk (hence the
> decksize being dependent on how many players there were) I think it's
> fair to assume that the amount of cards has been the result of
> playing, and seeing how many cards were played, then a simplification
> of that.

They probably decided that running out of cards needed to be a risk
because of two things - they wanted to avoid having a card limit, and
they wanted cards to replace immediately. It's not terribly hard to
burn through 10+ cards in a turn, and unlike most CCGs, you'll still
have a full hand of 7 when you're done, instead of having to rebuild
your hand over several turns. So by limiting deck size, you're still
forced to manage your cards wisely, instead of just building a giant
deck and playing as fast as possible.

> So the original rules stated: 40+10/player is the maximum size.

40 likely being a holdover from magic, and 10 per player allows people
to build 60-card decks for 2-player games. 60 is a nice round number
that people would be used to if they played in any magic tournaments.

> However, since in a tournament it isnt a good idea to have people
> alter their decks between rounds based on how many players they have
> to play against, a basic standard had to be set, in accordance to the
> rules above, taking into account the tournament maximum of players/
> table is 5, the upper limit was set at 90.
> Since the minimum amount of players to play the game is 2, the lower
> limit is 60.

The upper limit did need to remain constant across the tournament,
hence 90 (allowing people to have enough cards for their 5-player
games was presumably deemed more important than being restricted in
your 4-player games).

60 is likely a holdover from magic, rather than actually being a
meaningful number on it's own (or perhaps, it's just as meaningful as
it is in magic, and was for that reason held over).

witness1

Messages.Body:
In article <1182863792.8...@p77g2000hsh.googlegroups.com>,
witness1 <jwnew...@bellsouth.net> wrote:

> 60 is likely a holdover from magic, rather than actually being a
> meaningful number on it's own (or perhaps, it's just as meaningful as
> it is in magic, and was for that reason held over).

It is both a holdover from Magic (as noted by a few others) due to the
DCI having come up with the original tournament rules and also probably
(also from Magic) an attempt to minimize "degenerate" deck building,
which, also as noted, is mostly moot now due to the existence of burn
option cards (i.e. build a 30 card deck and pad it out with 30 burn
option cards. Or 30 Zip Guns, heh.)

The only CCG I have run into with no deck size limits is Shadowfist
(which does have a per card 5CL)--you can play a 6 card deck if you
really want (T1: "I play a Feng Shui Site and a Friends of the Dragon.
I, uh, have no deck left. I lose.")
